questions.stem: A student wants to make pure, dry copper sulfate crystals from copper oxide and sulfuric acid. She adds excess copper oxide to warm acid, then filters. Why must she add excess copper oxide?

options.text: To make the reaction happen faster
To produce more copper sulfate
To ensure all the acid is used up, so the salt is not contaminated with acid
To act as a catalyst

questions.explanation: If any unreacted acid remains, the solution would be acidic and impure. Adding excess insoluble base (copper oxide) ensures all the acid reacts. The excess copper oxide is then removed by filtration because it is insoluble. The filtrate contains only pure copper sulfate solution, which can be crystallised.

questions.stem: After filtering off excess copper oxide, a student has a blue copper sulfate solution. What should she do next to obtain dry crystals?

options.text: Boil the solution rapidly until completely dry
Gently evaporate some water, then leave to cool and crystallise; dry crystals with filter paper
Add more copper oxide to the solution
Pour the solution into a freezer

questions.explanation: Gently heating evaporates some water to make a saturated solution (test by dipping a glass rod - if crystals form on it, the solution is saturated). Then leave to cool slowly - crystals form as the solution cools because it can hold less dissolved salt at lower temperatures. Finally, filter and pat dry. Rapid boiling would produce small, powdery crystals or decompose the salt.

questions.stem: To make sodium chloride from hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide, the excess base method cannot be used because NaOH is soluble. What method should be used instead?

options.text: Add excess sodium hydroxide and filter off the excess
Titration - use a burette to add exact amounts, then evaporate to crystallise
Heat the acid until it evaporates, leaving the salt behind
Mix equal volumes of any concentrations of acid and alkali

questions.explanation: Since NaOH is soluble, it cannot be filtered off if added in excess. Instead, a titration is used to find the exact volume of NaOH needed to neutralise the acid (using an indicator). Then the experiment is repeated without indicator using these exact volumes. The resulting neutral solution is evaporated to obtain pure NaCl crystals.

questions.stem: A student wants to prepare magnesium sulfate. Which of the following starting materials and methods would work?

options.text: Magnesium ribbon + dilute nitric acid
Magnesium oxide + dilute sulfuric acid
Magnesium chloride + sodium sulfate
Magnesium + water

questions.explanation: To make magnesium sulfate, you need a magnesium compound reacting with sulfuric acid (which provides the sulfate). MgO + H2SO4 -> MgSO4 + H2O. Option A would produce magnesium nitrate (wrong acid). Option C could work via double decomposition if one product is insoluble, but MgSO4 and NaCl are both soluble. Option D would produce Mg(OH)2, not a sulfate.

questions.stem: Which of the following insoluble substances could NOT be used to make a soluble salt by the excess solid method with dilute hydrochloric acid?

options.text: Zinc oxide
Copper carbonate
Sodium hydroxide
Iron powder

questions.explanation: The excess solid method requires adding an INSOLUBLE excess reactant that can be filtered off. Sodium hydroxide is soluble, so any excess would remain in solution and contaminate the salt. Zinc oxide, copper carbonate, and iron are all insoluble in water and can be added in excess, with the unreacted portion removed by filtration.
